facts.text: To relieve tension on set, writer-director-star Neil Breen reportedly played a pair of bongos while wearing a Bigfoot suit.
The desert scenery was shot at Nelson Ghost Town in Clark County, Nevada, an abandoned gold-mining site that's a favorite spot for photographers.
Pass Thru's first public showing was a one-night-only screening on April 19, 2016 at the Capitol Theatre in Cleveland, Ohio, according to Cleveland Scene and Letterboxd.
Pass Thru was Neil Breen's fourth film and his first to use crowdfunding. Breen said he already had enough money and used it just to improve the final product.
Pass Thru hit DVD in the USA on October 20, 2016, unrated, about six months after its Cleveland theatrical showing.
Neil Breen pays for his films from his earnings as a professional architect, using amateur casts and crews. His website calls him 'the most independent filmmaker in the world.'
Cleveland Scene's listing called Pass Thru 'an inept metaphysical dram-com' for fans of The Room, yet said writer-director-star Neil Breen is 'by all accounts sincere in his efforts.'
Neil Breen's films have a cult following as 'so bad it's good' cinema, and he is often compared to Tommy Wiseau, the director and star of The Room.
Cleveland Scene reported that Neil Breen, a Las Vegas architect, rejects labels like 'cult' and 'late-night' for his movies. He means them sincerely.
Neil Breen has never gone to film school. He told CineDump: 'Making Double Down WAS my film school.' That was his 2005 debut, eleven years before Pass Thru.
Goof spotters note the heroin-injection moment shows liquid simply being sprayed onto the arm, with brown spots of makeup standing in for old needle marks.
Despite the home-made vibe, filmmaker Neil Breen told CineDump that everyone, cast and crew, on all of his films has been paid. He rejects the idea that they're friends doing favors.
Neil Breen's credits list him as writer, director, producer, editor, star, musical director, cinematographer, production designer and more. Basically, he is the crew.
Neil Breen told Whopperjaw he cast locally, with all cast and crew from Nevada. For older roles he looked for faces 'full of wrinkles' and 'scratchy voices.'
Breen's debut, Double Down (2005), was later featured on RedLetterMedia's Best of the Worst series. RedLetterMedia also covered his later film Fateful Findings on YouTube.
Wikipedia's Neil Breen entry says the architect-turned-director has said he recruited cast members through Craigslist ads, so many of his actors are amateurs.
Los Angeles cinematheque Cinefamily screened Neil Breen's Double Down in 2010 and I Am Here.... Now in 2011, helping launch his midnight-movie cult.
Neil Breen told CineDump he writes scripts around his money: 'I knew what my budget was. I knew what my geographic restrictions were.' That's why his films keep returning to the desert.
Goof spotters point out the news anchors here say 'bias' and 'prejudice' as if they were adjectives. Both are nouns.
Neil Breen told Whopperjaw that audiences start by chuckling, go quiet, and by the end 'they're giving it a standing ovation.' He says Q&As with 150 fans are a great feeling.
Pass Thru is name-checked in other movies, including Suicide Squad (2016), Vanity Project (2020) and Birdemic 3: Sea Eagle, per IMDb's connections list.

The Chicken Dynasty review notes the corrupt-executives party is visibly green screen. HorrorNews.net's Charleston Picou likened the film's backgrounds to the prerendered ones in 1996's Resident Evil.
Breen's films reuse a formula: an angry entity tries to cleanse the world, with stock footage and long monologues about the news. Pass Thru has its own site, pass-thru-film.com.
The Chicken Dynasty blog gave Pass Thru 2 out of 5 eggs. It said the film looks like a bigger-budget version of Neil Breen's 2009 movie I Am Here.... Now.
Blogger Connor Tumbleson found that Pass Thru DVDs were sold through PayPal links for $25.95, shipped by USPS in 3 to 4 weeks, with no artwork or subtitles.
The comedy podcast The Worst Idea of All Time reviewed Pass Thru: recorded for Patreon in December 2017, released publicly May 14, 2018. It called the film 'one for the books.'
Paste magazine ranked Breen's I Am Here.... Now number 21 on its 2014 list of the 100 best B movies.
Neil Breen's films have played festivals and cult venues, including the 2012 Butt-Numb-A-Thon and the 2013 Seattle International Film Festival.
A denim military vest from Breen's debut Double Down (2005), tied to a character named Aaron Brand, is carried around as a prop late in Pass Thru.
Neil Breen kept going: Cade: The Tortured Crossing (2023) played Alamo Drafthouse theaters nationwide, and his seventh feature, Dire Duplicity, was set for Alamo rollout in September 2026.
Breen's earlier film Fateful Findings had a North American distributor, Panorama Entertainment, which compared it to Tommy Wiseau's cult classic The Room.
The credits claim any company with an 'N' or 'B' in its name is fictitious and that the work was 'actually done personally by Neil Breen.' N and B are Breen's initials.
